item.title: Why One Case of Psychosis Cannot Define the Illness
item.description:
Psychosis

Why One Case of Psychosis Cannot Define the Illness

Research shows most people with psychotic disorders are not violent.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Being psychotic does not automatically make a person violent.
  • Selective exposure in the media helps drive the belief that most cases of psychosis involve violence.
  • Cutting support based on rare violent cases risks undermining recovery and worsening outcomes.
Source: AdobeStock / timitinej

We must be careful not to let one case define psychosis in general, as each case of psychosis can be as unique and varied as fingerprints. Psychosis can draw from and play upon your deepest insecurities, memories, and relationships in a way that is deeply personal and customized. Alternate realities and false narratives are created by your brain through reshuffling what it has already experienced, and it seems 100 percent real.

Psychosis can present in infinite variations that are categorically different, so to learn of one publicized case and apply that understanding to all cases of psychosis is misguided and harmful for the vast majority of people who experience psychosis. One may assume that one case of psychosis is just like any other, but that is not correct. We should not define, judge, or epitomize an illness through one instance of psychosis and make decisions and judgments for everyone with that illness accordingly.

Every Case Is Different Based on Numerous Factors

Psychosis as a mental health condition is diverse and varied in many ways. There are psychotic-like elements (PLEs), one-time breaks, and chronic disorders. Cases range from mild to severe.

Some people black out, and others remember everything. Some have insight that they are experiencing psychotic symptoms, while others do not.

Some people hear voices, and others don’t. Some elements of psychosis, like hallucinations, can be friendly and helpful, but others can be mean and scary. Some people have psychosis for days, some for weeks, some for months, and some for years.

Some people can manage at home under careful supervision of family, and others need to commit themselves to a psych ward. Some people just need to be in an emergency psych ward to recover, while others need to be institutionalized in a state hospital.

Some people choose medicine, and others are determined to go without it. Some people experience debilitating side effects from antipsychotics and cannot get them resolved, while other people have milder side effects and can manage them. Antipsychotics offer a good prognosis to a third of patients, a moderate prognosis to the middle third, and then a poor prognosis to the last third.

Psychosis and psychotic symptoms can be caused by many other medical conditions besides SMI diagnoses, including, but not limited to: thyroid diseases, urinary tract infections, brain tumors, systemic infections like HIV, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis, vitamin deficiencies, and lupus.

article continues after advertisement

The Issue of Violence vs. Nonviolence

Perhaps the most debated and misunderstood difference among psychosis cases is the likelihood of violence. It is possible to break the law during a psychotic break, and in rare cases, violence like homicide occurs. However, the tendency to think that anyone psychotic is instantly dangerous is misguided and incorrect. In fact, 80 to 90 percent of people with a psychotic disorder are not violent at all, and I am an example of total nonviolence.

I was diagnosed with schizophrenia 15 years ago, and have been completely symptom-free, meaning literally zero mental health symptoms, for at least 13 years. I remember everything from each of my four psychotic breaks, and not once did I have a single violent word, thought, impulse, behavior, or desire. I do not have any violent inclinations in remission, either. I gave birth to a son during full recovery, and I can assure you I am no different than any other mother.

The Ultimate Tragedy: If We All Lost Support and Resources

More people fully recover from psychotic disorders than ever before, including schizophrenia, due to improved medication options, therapies, and resources in general. The World Health Organization states online that a third of all schizophrenia cases fully recover.[1] I am an example of someone who lives 100 percent mental illness-free while on antipsychotic medication for life.

It would be the greatest tragedy for any one case of the illness to influence support and resources for people with psychosis in a negative way. The existing support system and resources saved my life and made it possible for me to still achieve my life dreams and also give back to the mental health community. Furthermore, withdrawing support and resources for people with psychosis would just guarantee more tragedies like the ones that make national headlines.

Why You Don’t Hear Many Positive Success Stories

I know there are a lot more people like me who just aren’t public about their illness like I am. If you are fully recovered, there is no motivation or benefit whatsoever to sharing a stigmatized diagnosis and painful experiences if you don’t need to apply for work accommodations or explain any existing symptoms in social relationships.

article continues after advertisement

Because of this, though, there are limited means to learn of a sufficient number of cases of psychosis and see how they vary, as well as see how the vast majority are nonviolent. Unfortunately for most of the public, their only exposure is what is presented in the media, where selective exposure on cases involving homicide is the norm. The media is less likely to cover a positive success story like mine, because a rare story covering homicide that feeds on fear and typical stereotypes gains higher readership.

To illustrate just how rare violence is associated with schizophrenia and related disorders, here are the latest facts, so we don’t generalize about psychosis based on one instance of the illness.

Essential Statistics on Psychosis and Nonviolence

  1. The chances of being murdered by someone with psychosis (who you don’t personally know) are 1 in 14.3 million.[2]
  2. A person with schizophrenia is 14 times more likely to be a victim of violence compared to being arrested as a perpetrator.[3]
  3. Schizophrenia is linked to 6.48 percent of worldwide homicides according to one study[4], while another study confirms that 95 percent of all homicides linked to schizophrenia co-occur with substance abuse.[5] If you take these two results together, what this means is that schizophrenia by itself (without substance abuse) is linked to only 0.324 percent of annual global murders.
  4. The likelihood for violence in someone with schizophrenia with co-occurring substance abuse is similar to that for substance abuse without psychosis.[6]
  5. Columbia University and the New York Psychiatric Institute partner to manage the world’s largest database on mass murder. In one study evaluating approximately 855 mass shootings (65 percent of 1315 mass murders analyzed were shootings), "active psychotic symptoms" were identified in only 5 percent of these mass shooters. This paper concludes “that policies aimed at preventing mass shootings by focusing on serious mental illness, characterized by psychotic symptoms, may have limited impact.”[7]
article continues after advertisement

Following one publicized case is not an accurate means to learn what psychosis is like for everyone who has it. I hope these facts reassure you that we are categorically nonviolent, and truly learning more about psychosis requires a case-by-case evaluation.

item.title: Why You Feel the Sunday Scaries and What to Do About Them
item.description:
Career

Why You Feel the Sunday Scaries and What to Do About Them

When your body is still in Sunday, but your brain is already in Monday.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • The Sunday scaries are a form of anticipatory stress.
  • Small, intentional practices can help ease the transition into a new week and give Sunday back to you.
  • Persistent Sunday dread may be a signal that something needs to change.

It's Sunday afternoon. You've finally checked off all the things keeping your life outside work afloat, so you exhale, but the rest is short-lived. An old, familiar, yet unwelcome feeling starts to grow. You notice a shorter fuse with the people you love. Your mood plummets as your mind races and your anxiety spikes. That's when you know, as if on cue, the Sunday scaries are back.

What Are the Sunday Scaries?

The Sunday scaries are this creeping sense of dread, anxiety, or uneasiness that shows up as the weekend winds down. It is what we call "anticipatory stress," a reaction to what we think is coming, not necessarily to what is happening right now.

For some, it can show up as irritability or a mind that won't slow down. For others, it might be trouble falling asleep or a heavy sense of dread within. Whatever form they take, they are a familiar emotional reality and experience for many, and they're not always just about work. Children, students, parents, and caregivers can experience their own version of the Sunday scaries as they anticipate what's ahead. For strategies to help children cope, I invite you to read my previous post.

Why We Get the Sunday Scaries

Our brains are constantly scanning ahead, trying to anticipate challenges and keep us safe. Worries about workload, balancing personal and professional to-dos, and carrying unfinished tasks into a new week are all commonly reported as contributing to the familiar sense of unease. A recent study out of the University of Exeter found that 79% of people experience or have experienced the "Sunday Night Blues" at some point (Inceoglu et al., 2025). Energy was lowest on Sunday evening, even lower than on Monday evening. Research has also found that subjective well-being can decline as the weekend draws to a close (Akay & Martinsson, 2009). Participants in another qualitative study described how the feeling can spread through a household (Peng et al., 2026).

There are three things that tend to drive the Sunday scaries:

  • Uncertainty: We don’t know what the week will bring, so our minds fill in the blanks.
  • Loss of control: Our cognitive load may ease over the weekend, making the thought of juggling competing priorities, obligations, decisions, and demands and transitioning into work mode feel especially daunting.
  • The pressure to perform: We feel we must be ready to do it all again, sometimes even before we’ve recovered from the previous week, and if the weekend hasn’t brought the rest or enjoyment we hoped for, we may start the week feeling weary and depleted rather than refreshed.
article continues after advertisement

If the dread is persistent, getting curious about where it is stemming from can be helpful, whether it's an unsustainable workload, a difficult boss, a lack of recognition, or work that no longer feels meaningful or challenging. There are things we can do to care for our well-being, while also recognizing when it's something about the work that needs to change.

What We Can Do About Them

Here are five ways we can start to ease the anxiety and make the transition into a new week feel a little easier.

Name the feeling and stressor: Naming the feeling as specifically as we can and identifying the stressor helps us move it from a looming feeling to a problem we can understand. Ask yourself: Where do I feel this in my body? What am I worried about? Sometimes there is one clear cause, like a presentation or a difficult conversation, while other times it is many smaller things stacked on top of one another. Our nervous system will give us signals and clues that are worth paying attention to. It is our job to use that as information.

Make Monday smaller: Trying to tackle the whole week on Sunday night can feel like a losing battle. Before signing off on Friday, jot down your top three tasks for Monday so they are waiting on paper, not circling in your head. Then, I invite you to think of the week as a seven-game series. One day at a time, and let's aim for four wins!

Build self-trust, not just a better to-do list: Instead of spending Sunday evening trying to anticipate every possible problem in an attempt to feel more in control, try reminding yourself of the challenges you have already navigated and the skills you have developed. You don't need to know exactly how the week will unfold to trust that you can respond as it does.

article continues after advertisement

Give Sunday something to look forward to: Start a running "joy playbook" on your phone or in a notebook, filled with the people, places, hobbies, and little rituals that give you a little lift. Each Sunday, pick one to enjoy. Perhaps for you it could look like a walk, a favourite show, or cozying up with a good book. You can even get the whole family involved!

Call it what it is: Not every job has to be your dream job, and not every career has to last forever. Sometimes you're learning, sometimes you're earning. Reminding yourself what this role is making possible, and having a plan for what comes next, can make the temporary feel less daunting. If the dread shows up week after week, it is worth taking a closer look at whether the role is a good fit and still aligns with your values.

What works for one person may not work for someone else. My gentle invitation is to notice how these practices feel for you and keep what helps.

Final Thoughts

Sunday is a day of your life, not just a waiting room for Monday. When it's spent bracing for the week ahead, we miss the chance to truly slow down, recharge, and make what matters most matter most. Remember, too, that worrying about the week ahead isn't the same as preparing for it. Worry tends to go in circles, while preparation gives us something to act on. If something pops up, ask yourself if there's something small you can do about it right now to put the worry to rest. If not, write it on a sticky note and tell yourself you will address it on Monday.

Our work matters, but it should never matter more than the person doing it. Taking care of ourselves is part of what helps us continue to do the good work and show up for the people who count on us, personally and professionally.
